name: Yusuf Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Yusuf. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a CNC lathe at Kessler Components, which makes brake pistons for car makers. CNC means the lathe is computer controlled, so I load the steel bar, call up the program, and watch it cut. Then I measure parts with a micrometer every twenty pieces and log them. I'm still slow on changeovers, when you swap the tools and the program for a different part, and the older guys are twice as quick.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, who's at home and how's money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: What I like is that it's half machine and half puzzle. I use an AI chat tool on my phone at break almost every day to explain bits of the G-code, which is the language the lathe reads, and it's taught me more than the induction did. What wears me out is the twelve-hour weekend shifts in the busy months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bit of a let-down, honestly. I'm the one at work who's always showing people what the AI can do, so I'd get some stick in the break room if it turned out to be hype. Online I'd say the tools are still useful even if they're not magic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's probably fine for me. Kessler has steady orders, and a lathe operator who can actually read the code is worth keeping. My savings are about four months, so I'm not on the edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the chat tool to learn the programs, because that's still how I get better fastest. I'd ask my supervisor, Joe, to let me do my own changeovers on the night shift. And I'd keep putting a bit aside each month, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, maybe a bit bored. It's the world I already live in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about Kessler that does worry you, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car makers keep switching to electric, and electric cars use fewer of our brake parts. That's a slow thing, though, years not months. Joe says they're already quoting for battery housings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Amira say about your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Amira, my girlfriend, is a dental nurse and she thinks I should go for an engineering apprenticeship. She's probably right. In the boring version of the future I'd still do it, just slower.

say: I'd say it's a **let-down**, and take some teasing in the break room.
Online I'd say the tools are still **useful, not magic**.
think: Privately, my job looks **steady**, because Kessler has orders and needs code-readers.
With about **four months saved**, I'm not close to the edge.
do: Keep using **the chat tool** at break to learn the lathe programs.
Ask Joe (my supervisor) to let me run **my own changeovers** on nights.
Put a little aside **each month** without changing much else.
feel: **Calm** and a bit bored, because this is the world I already know.
S0.quote: I'm the one at work who's always showing people what the AI can do, so I'd get some stick in the break room if it turned out to be hype.
fieldNote: He is the **early adopter** on his shift and enjoys that role.
His real slow worry is **electric cars** cutting brake part orders.
Amira (his girlfriend) pushes him towards **an apprenticeship**, which he half agrees with.

steps.text: Ask Joe for solo changeovers on the night shift
Use the AI chat tool at break to decode G-code programs
Set aside a small sum from each monthly payslip

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to get ahead, not hide. At work I'd tell people to learn the new screens now, while the bosses still want our input. Online I'd push for the union to get training budgets in the next contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the people who programme and fix machines will do fine, and the people who only load them won't. Right now I'm closer to the loaders than the programmers. That's the honest bit that bothers me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for an evening course in CNC programming at the college this winter, about eight hundred in fees. I'd use AI tools every day to practise writing programs on the simulator at home. And I'd tell the union rep we want a training clause, because not everyone can pay for courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a fired-up way. I can see where I need to get to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stan, who's done the same job for thirty years and won't touch a tablet. He's brilliant with his hands, but the new quality software will drive him mad. I'd try to help him, but I can't make him want to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your savings with an eight-hundred course fee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd drop to about three months, which is fine. Amira and I would skip the summer trip for one year. I'd rather spend on a skill than a beach.

Online I'd push the union for **training budgets** in the next contract.
think: Privately, people who **programme and fix** machines will do fine, but loaders won't.
Right now I'm closer to **the loaders**, and that bothers me.
do: Sign up for an evening **CNC programming course** this winter for about eight hundred.
Practise writing programs on **a home simulator** with AI tools every day.
Ask the union rep for **a training clause** in the next contract.
feel: **Uneasy but fired up**, because I can see where I need to get to.
S1.quote: The people who programme and fix machines will do fine, and the people who only load them won't. Right now I'm closer to the loaders than the programmers.
fieldNote: He is frank that his **current skill level** puts him on the wrong side.
His answer is to **spend savings on skills** rather than cut back.
He worries about Stan (an older colleague) more than **about himself**.

steps.text: Pay about eight hundred for an evening CNC programming course
Practise lathe programs on a home simulator with AI help
Ask the union rep to push for a training clause
Skip the summer trip with Amira for one year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a robot dividend: if machines do the work, some of the profit comes back to people. I'd post that and argue for it. At work I'd say don't panic, but don't wait either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the thinking side of the lathe goes in 2028, so programming won't be a safe place to hide. I'd have about three years until robots can do the loading and measuring too. That's a short runway for someone who's still slow on changeovers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd switch from the programming course to robot maintenance, because someone still has to fix the robots in 2031. I'd push savings up to six months by cutting takeaways and the car loan if I can. In the first year after AGI arrives, I'd apply to the robot makers themselves as an installer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Exciting and frightening at the same time, but more frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap between the AI and the robots change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes what I study. If AI does the code in 2028, coding is pointless. Learning to fix arms and sensors buys me three years, and the hands are the last bit to go. Maybe more than three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Amira that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Amira that her job at the dentist is probably safer than mine, which would be a first. Then we'd talk about whether to wait on moving in together properly. I'd want to know my income first.

say: I'd argue for **a robot dividend**, so some machine profit comes back to people.
At work I'd say **don't panic**, but don't wait either.
think: Privately, **programming** won't be a safe hiding place once AI does it in 2028.
I'd have about **three years** before robots load and measure parts too.
do: Switch from programming to a **robot maintenance course** straight away.
Push savings to **six months** by cutting takeaways and the car loan.
Apply to **robot makers** as an installer in the first year after AGI.
feel: **Anxious**, a mix of excitement and fear with fear on top.
S2.quote: If AI does the code in 2028, coding is pointless. Learning to fix arms and sensors buys me three years, and the hands are the last bit to go.
fieldNote: He uses the **robot delay** to pick what to study, not just to feel safer.
Even for an adaptive worker, **three years** feels short at his skill level.
He would hold **moving in** with Amira (his girlfriend) until his income is clearer.

steps.text: Switch to a robot maintenance course at the college
Cut takeaways and pay off the car loan to reach six months saved
Apply to robot makers as an installer after AGI arrives
Post and argue online for a robot dividend

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to fix the system if politicians start now. I'd push the union to plan a shorter working week, so fewer jobs are lost. Online I'd keep it practical: here's what to study, here's where the courses are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is good for me. Robots on the line by 2034 gives me about eight years in total, long enough to become the person who installs and fixes them. I'm adaptive, so I'd rather be early to that than late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd finish the CNC programming course, then start robot maintenance in year two. I'd ask Kessler to put me on the commissioning team when the next robot cell arrives. I'd keep saving about a hundred and fifty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly in a hopeful way. I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Kessler doesn't put you on the commissioning team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go somewhere that would. There are three other plants within half an hour of me, and one of them is putting in robot cells now. I wouldn't wait around to be asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you worry about your friends from school?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A couple of them work in a warehouse, picking and packing. Robots will be all over that by 2034. I'd send them the course links, but they'd probably laugh at me.

say: I'd say five years is enough **if politicians start now**.
I'd push the union for **a shorter working week** to spread the work.
think: Privately, robots by **2034** gives me about eight years to become the fixer.
Being **adaptive**, I'd rather arrive early than late.
do: Finish the **CNC programming course** this year, then start robot maintenance.
Ask Kessler to put me on **the commissioning team** for the next robot cell.
Keep saving about **a hundred and fifty** a month.
feel: **Uneasy but hopeful**, and I'd sleep fine.
S3.quote: There are three other plants within half an hour of me, and one of them is putting in robot cells now. I wouldn't wait around to be asked.
fieldNote: He treats the extra years as **a career ladder**, not a reprieve.
Local plants give him **real options**, which keeps his mood steady.
His worry turns outward to **school friends** in warehouse jobs.

steps.text: Finish the CNC programming course, then start robot maintenance
Volunteer for Kessler's robot cell commissioning team
Apply to the nearby plant installing robot cells if refused
Push the union to plan for a shorter working week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd be stupid to waste it. At work I'd say this is the time for everyone to pick a second skill. Online I'd talk about the shorter week and public training again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this is my best case. Robots on the line by 2039 means I'd be thirty-nine, probably a technician or running a robot cell by then. I'd be on the right side of it if I keep going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the CNC course this year, an engineering apprenticeship after that, and maybe a robotics certificate around 2030. Amira and I would move in together properly next year and start saving for a deposit. I'd keep using AI tools every day, because they'd keep getting better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit excited, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version of this where you get it wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I get lazy, yes. Ten years is long enough to drift, and I've seen guys at my plant promise a course for five years running. I'd set myself deadlines and tell my girlfriend. Amira would nag me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should pay for all the retraining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the companies that save money from the robots, and the government should fill the gaps. Workers shouldn't have to spend their savings to stay employable. I'm lucky I can, but plenty can't.

I'd tell people at work to **pick a second skill** now.
think: Privately, this is **my best case**, with robots on the line by 2039.

feel: **Calm** and a little excited about what's possible.

fieldNote: The long warning makes him **calm**, because his plan fits the timeline.

steps.text: Start an engineering apprenticeship after finishing the CNC course

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be learning to fix robots while also trying to keep my job, with no slack. What would help is free robot maintenance courses in the evening, and the union making sure plants hire their own operators to look after the new cells first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that. Half my shift asks the AI chat tool things on their phones and just doesn't tell the bosses. You'd be surprised how many of us use it already.

headlineQuote: Half my shift asks the AI chat tool things on their phones and just doesn't tell the bosses. You'd be surprised how many of us use it already.
portrait: Yusuf is a **27-year-old CNC lathe operator** at a brake parts plant, still slow on changeovers.
He uses an **AI chat tool** daily to learn the lathe code and enjoys being the early adopter.
He lives with plans to move in with **Amira (his girlfriend)**, a dental nurse, and has about four months saved.
His politics favour **a robot dividend**, shorter weeks and union training clauses.
He stays **calm to uneasy** except at AGI by 2028, where three years feels too short.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd be retraining with no slack while his job shrinks.
whatWouldHelp: Plants hiring **their own operators** to run new robot cells first.
